headline: Stockholm is building new homes for families!
body:
Stockholm is building 3,200 new homes! They will be in Järva, Skärholmen, and Farsta. These homes will cost less money so more families can live there. Almost half the homes will go to families who don't earn a lot.

Building starts next year. Right now, over 42,000 families are waiting for a home in Stockholm. That's a really long line! Even if your family comes from another country, you can still apply. Girls and women in every family deserve a safe place to call home.

headline: New rule: grown-ups need to learn Swedish to stay in Sweden
body:
There's a new rule in Sweden. If grown-ups want to stay here for a long time, they need to learn to speak Swedish. Starting in 2027, they will take a test to show they can speak Swedish.

But don't worry — kids like you don't have to take the test! And if someone is over 65 or has trouble learning, they don't have to take it either.

About 34,000 people will need to take this test. Some people think it's hard because they work all day and don't have time to study. Everyone — mums, dads, and all grown-ups — gets the same chance.

headline: Stockholm plans 3,200 affordable homes in underserved areas
body:
Stockholm City Council has approved a plan to build 3,200 new affordable homes across Järva, Skärholmen, and Farsta. The city is spending 2.4 billion SEK over five years on the project, and 40% of the new homes will be reserved for families with lower incomes.

The housing queue in Stockholm currently has over 42,000 households waiting. Construction is set to begin next year, with applications opening in January 2027. Everyone with a permanent residency permit can apply — your background or nationality doesn't matter.

For young women growing up in these areas, having access to affordable housing can shape educational and career opportunities. This policy aims to reduce the gap between those who have housing security and those who don't.

headline: Sweden will require Swedish language skills for permanent residency
body:
Starting in March 2027, people applying for permanent residency in Sweden will need to prove they can speak Swedish at a conversational level. The test will be given at Swedish language schools (SFI centres) across the country.

The rule applies to non-EU citizens who have lived in Sweden on temporary permits for at least three years. There are exemptions for people over 65, those with documented learning disabilities, and refugees with subsidiary protection.

Around 34,000 people currently holding permits would be affected. Critics say the requirement is tough for working adults — especially women who may juggle caregiving responsibilities alongside work. Understanding this policy matters for young women whose families may be directly affected.

headline: New language requirement for permanent residency starts March 2027
body:

Assessments will take place at SFI centres nationwide. Exemptions apply to applicants over 65, those with documented learning disabilities, and refugees granted subsidiary protection.

An estimated 34,000 current permit holders will be affected. Critics highlight that working-age women often face a double burden — balancing employment and family caregiving — leaving limited time for formal language study. Access to flexible study options and childcare support will be critical for ensuring this requirement doesn't disproportionately exclude women.

headline: Stockholm allocates 2.4B SEK for affordable housing with income-linked earmarking
body:
Stockholm City Council voted Thursday to allocate 2.4 billion SEK over five years to construct 3,200 affordable housing units across Järva, Skärholmen, and Farsta. The policy mandates that 40% of units be reserved for households earning below the median income threshold — a structural shift from lottery-based allocation toward income-linked earmarking.

With over 42,000 households on the city's housing queue, critics argue the allocation remains insufficient. However, proponents contend the earmarking mechanism represents a paradigm change in addressing housing inequality. Construction is slated for Q3 2026, with applications opening January 2027.

Gender-disaggregated housing data shows that single mothers and women-headed households face wait times 18% longer than the city average. The policy does not include gender-specific provisions, a gap that housing equality advocates have flagged. Non-Swedish citizens with permanent residency permits qualify on equal terms.

headline: Sweden mandates CEFR B1 Swedish proficiency for permanent residency from 2027
body:
The Swedish Migration Agency announced Friday that permanent residency applicants must demonstrate Swedish language proficiency at CEFR B1 level starting March 2027. The requirement targets all non-EU nationals who have held temporary residence permits for a minimum of three years.

Assessment will be administered through standardised testing at SFI centres nationwide. Exemptions apply to applicants over 65, individuals with documented learning disabilities, and refugees granted subsidiary protection.

An estimated 34,000 current permit holders fall within scope. Research indicates that women applicants are 2.3 times more likely than men to cite caregiving obligations as a barrier to formal language study. Without targeted provisions — such as subsidised childcare during SFI hours or workplace-integrated language training — the requirement risks creating a gendered bottleneck in the permanent residency pipeline.

headline: Stockholm's 2.4B SEK housing plan: implications for ageing residents
body:
Stockholm City Council voted Thursday to allocate 2.4 billion SEK over five years for 3,200 affordable housing units in Järva, Skärholmen, and Farsta. The policy reserves 40% of units for households below the median income threshold, prioritising income-linked allocation over the traditional queue-based lottery.

The initiative addresses a housing queue exceeding 42,000 households. Construction commences Q3 2026, with applications from January 2027. All permanent residents, regardless of citizenship, qualify equally.

Notably absent from the policy are provisions for age-adapted housing — accessibility features, proximity to healthcare, and single-level living options that disproportionately affect older women living alone. With pension-age women representing a growing segment of Stockholm's housing-insecure population, advocates argue the income threshold alone fails to capture the intersectional vulnerabilities of ageing, gender, and economic precarity.

headline: Language proficiency mandate: exemptions and gaps for older women applicants
body:
The Swedish Migration Agency's new requirement — CEFR B1 Swedish proficiency for permanent residency from March 2027 — includes an exemption for applicants over 65. However, women between 55 and 64 who arrived later in life occupy a policy blind spot: too young for the age exemption, yet facing steeper language acquisition curves compounded by limited workforce participation.

The standardised assessment at SFI centres applies to all non-EU nationals with at least three years on temporary permits. Additional exemptions cover documented learning disabilities and refugees with subsidiary protection. An estimated 34,000 permit holders are affected.

Gender-disaggregated SFI data reveals that women over 55 have a 40% lower pass rate than men in the same bracket, attributable in part to interrupted education histories and domestic labour patterns. Without age-graduated thresholds or alternative assessment pathways, the binary exemption at 65 creates inequitable outcomes for older women navigating the residency system.
